![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-

Photo by [engin
akyurt](https://unsplash.com/@enginakyurt?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText)

Our world is awash in plastic. From single-use [water
bottles](https://cleantechnica.com/2025/12/07/your-single-use-plastic-bottles-
are-killing-endangered-sea-turtles/#google_vignette) and [food
packaging](https://www.nrdc.org/stories/single-use-plastics-101) to [synthetic
clothes](https://www.futurity.org/clothing-industry-plastic-
pollution-3261312/),
[shoes](https://www.asparagusmagazine.com/articles/reducing-plastic-pollution-
from-shoes-through-recycling-and-repair), and even [nail
polish](https://www.beatthemicrobead.org/project/nail-polish/), our
overreliance on plastic is spreading a toxic, [chemical-
laden](https://cen.acs.org/business/consumer-products/Plastic-food-packaging-
contains-thousands/102/web/2024/03) material all over the planet — including
in our own
[bodies](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2022/mar/24/microplastics-
found-in-human-blood-for-first-time).

Most Americans are sick of [plastic
use](https://www.dataforprogress.org/blog/2023/3/27/voters-express-concern-
about-plastic-pollution-strongly-support-mitigation-proposals), but
manufacturers continue to push the product on us. This holiday season, is it
possible to have a plastic-free celebration?

There’s no substitute for systemic policy change to regulate plastic use, but
individual actions on a mass scale can have an impact. They can also be a
dinner table conversation, potentially spurring cultural shifts and inspiring
local activism.

“None of us voted for more plastic,” [says Judith
Enck](https://risingupwithsonali.com/wishing-you-a-plastic-free-holiday-
season/), founder and president of [Beyond
Plastics](https://www.beyondplastics.org/?ref=risingupwithsonali.com). Enck,
who served as regional administrator at the Environmental Protection Agency in
2009, adds that “the reason we have so much plastic is because there is a glut
of [fracked
gas](https://www.plasticpollutioncoalition.org/blog/2024/9/17/fracked-gas-is-
a-growing-share-of-the-fossil-fuels-being-turned-into-plastics) on the
market.”

Enck says it’s entirely possible to have a plastic-free holiday season. She
suggests forgoing disposable dinnerware for your Christmas, Hannukah, or
Kwanzaa meal. “You can rent glassware and plates and beautiful reusable
tablecloths and napkins from local vendors,” she says.

The food at your holiday dinner table needn’t come packaged in plastic either.
Challenge yourself to purchase ingredients from your local farmers market
using cotton tote bags. Produce that is [locally
grown](https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/Why%20Local%20Food%20Matters.pdf)
is generally seasonal, tastier, has a lower carbon footprint, and is often
pesticide-free or organic.

Purchase drinks for your holiday dinner in glass bottles. Most wine is already
sold in glass, but even for teetotalers, it’s entirely possible to purchase
drinks packaged in glass bottles or cardboard boxes.

According to Enck, “materials like paper, cardboard, metal, and glass… can be
made of recycled material and actually does get recycled when you put it in
your recycling bin” — unlike plastic. Most plastic is [never
recycled](https://www.npr.org/2022/10/24/1131131088/recycling-plastic-is-
practically-impossible-and-the-problem-is-getting-worse), no matter how
diligent you are about cleaning and disposing of it in your recycling bins.

Gift-giving is particularly fraught with plastic. Mass-produced toys, clothes,
and gadgets are either made from plastic or wrapped in it. Enck’s organization
offers a handy [online guide](https://www.beyondplastics.org/holiday-
guides/holidaygiftguide) for plastic-free gifting, like giving memberships in
a [Community Supported Agriculture (CSA)
program](https://www.beyondplastics.org/holiday-guides/holidaygiftguide). Most
local communities, including cities, have local farmers who offer such
memberships.

“Consider giving experiences rather than material products,” she adds, like
“taking little kids to a matinee movie, giving your aunts and uncles tickets
to a concert or a play, or giving busy parents a couple coupons that you’ll go
and babysit their kids on a Saturday night.”

Memberships to museums, botanical gardens, and zoos are also excellent
alternatives to plastic products. A gift certificate for a massage or yoga
class for a busy working parent is likely to be received with far more
gratitude than yet another trinket they don’t need.

If you feel compelled to buy a product, there are sustainable alternatives.
Consider shopping at a thrift store to give an old product new life and save
it from the landfill. (Vintage items are always fashionable!) Find your local
“[Buy Nothing](https://buynothingproject.org/find-a-group)” groups and post a
request for lightly used items as gifts.

If you must purchase new gifts, consider plastic-free options. Clothing in
particular can be sustainable if it’s made with natural fibers such as cotton,
wool, or silk. Avoid clothes with
[labels](https://www.filtrol.net/post/microfiber-madness-how-to-spot-plastic-
in-your-clothing) marked polyester, poly-blend, nylon, acrylic, or microfiber.
Synthetic clothes are notorious for shedding microplastics that end up in our
blood stream and oceans.

Remember to use [recyclable gift
wrap](https://www.goodhousekeeping.com/holidays/christmas-ideas/g41170109/eco-
friendly-wrapping-
paper/?utm_source=google&utm_medium=cpc&utm_campaign=mgu_ga_ghk_md_pmx_hybd_mix_us_19597983321&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=19597985697&gbraid=0AAAAADA2MEpvBYvmLJrgepuxuCBT1l1mg&gclid=CjwKCAiA0eTJBhBaEiwA-
Pa-hf6s6V83jwWgE8JcKvp9fwui9n7t2xq8sS8DukeOtGLL6HcI-d1NahoCqxIQAvD_BwE),
wrapping paper alternatives like [tea
towels](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DRAwtMVEk-w/) or old cookie tins, or
simply reuse last year’s wrapping.

Most importantly, make your plastic-free (or plastic-light) holiday a talking
point at the dinner table and when exchanging gifts. These conversations can
lead to real change: Regulations such as [California’s new plastic bag
ban](https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/california-to-ban-all-
plastic-bags-at-retail-stores-
starting-2026/103-a873409f-ccb5-4f4b-b676-c5ae9060d6fc) and Georgia’s [plastic
food packaging ban](https://www.packaginginsights.com/news/georgia-plastic-
food-contact-ban.html) are set to take effect next year, and are the result of
[dedicated](https://www.plasticpollutioncoalition.org/blog/2025/10/21/big-win-
california-upholds-plastic-bag-ban)[ public
activism](https://gcvoters.org/blog/2022/02/18/the-problem-with-single-use-
plastics/).

Make a New Year’s resolution to commit to political action against plastic in
2026.
